en: In the commencement of affairs, there are diverse paths yet they share the same aim; people have different inclinations yet they follow the same practice.

Now, when Confucian scholars speak of immortality, they invariably say it consists of establishing virtue, establishing merit, and establishing words; and the Buddhists likewise have the Chan school, the Study (Doxography) school, and the Vinaya school.
It is said: Chan (meditation) approaches virtue; Vinaya (discipline) approaches merit; and Learning approaches words.

Yet, if one wishes to manifest virtue and emulate merit, to verify the present and leave a legacy for posterity, it cannot be accomplished without words. Looking at the establishment of words by the Confucians, I understand this:

when they first applied themselves with fervent resolve, they necessarily consulted the Classics, Histories, and the works of the hundred schools to exhaust their variations, and examined them through the lens of both Heaven and man.

One must penetrate the essentials of nature and destiny through the passage of years and months, allowing them to permeate one’s being without expecting rapid results; only then will there be attainment.

Yet, if one has still not achieved thorough penetration, one must embody the truth within oneself, so that the mind may understand and the spirit may harmonize with it, thereby returning to its original source.
Thus, there will be nothing that is not transformed. Only then can one begin to discern the truths spanning thousands and hundreds of years, both above and below.
I have minutely excavated the profound mysteries. At times I speak of what is near; at times I speak of what is distant.

Furthermore, I provide lateral expositions and indirect metaphors so that the world may clearly understand the sanctity of the author and so that I myself may not feel ashamed before the clarity of the commentator.
Thus these words are established; being established, they can be transmitted. Now, it is said that the Buddhist master Guanding ultimately found a point of convergence with this.

The Master was a student of the Buddha; his words differ from those of our Confucians. Yet, throughout his life, he neglected sleep and forgot to eat in his quest to reach the ground of establishing the ultimate teaching;
in this dedication of heart, he was also the same as our Confucians. At the age of nine, the Master entered the Gate of Emptiness.
At nineteen, he received the precepts; at twenty, he began the practice of lecturing on the sutras.
After seven years had passed, he received the formal entrustment (*parīndana*) from Master Deshui and became the fifth-generation Dharma descendant of Yunqi. Now, his age approaches eighty.

He has indeed frequently accepted invitations from scholars and officials, traveling through various monasteries such as Juguang and Tianzhu, proclaiming the subtle truth (*saddharma*) to enlighten the deaf and blind. Yet, he remains [as simple as] a blade of grass.
Wearing coarse garments and eating wood-shavings, he dwelt in seclusion within a small room. His hand never ceased its writing for fifty years.

The commentaries he authored on the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Vajracchedikā*, and other sutras total twenty-six works comprising one hundred and fifty fascicles; all of them penetrate deeply into the ocean of nature (*dharmatā*).
He has brought forth what the Teacher desired to bring forth, and he has further developed that which had not yet been developed.

I privately wish for his resolve to be firm and his accumulation of merit to be long-standing; had he exerted himself in the Confucian classics, he would have stood shoulder to shoulder with the various worthies of Changli and Luling, preceding or following them.
Yet, I alone regret that he ended his life as a Buddhist. Nevertheless, he cultivated the Brahma-conduct with refinement and elucidated...
In this world of five turbidities and evil, he has widely opened the path to awakening;

he is truly a successor to the Dharma King, what is known as the "Inexhaustible Lamp" that shines brightly and never ends. Jingyun, a monk of the doctrinal studies at Minzhong Temple in the capital, was my friend;
he traveled more than several thousand *li* to study under this master, and thus came to know the master’s life in its entirety. He compiled...
The number of woodblocks carved for this Great Canon of Śāstra commentaries from the ancient monastery of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* has been completed;
I have entrusted the temple monks with its preservation so that the Master’s established teachings may be transmitted. Therefore, I have composed this preface.
Preface composed and calligraphed by Wu Yongfang, Guardian of Jiahe and Protector of Silla, in the month of Qinghe, the fifty-eighth year of the Kangxi era (Jihai).
The Great Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty, lamenting the errors and corruptions in the scriptural texts, traveled throughout the Western regions for seventeen years.
He retrieved six hundred and fifty-seven volumes of scriptures and translated them at the Yuhua Palace. Emperor Taizong commanded his various civil officials:
He polished the text for them, beginning with the *Heart Sūtra*, and composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings" (*Shèngjiào xù*) to record it.

While the other translators were all from the Western Regions, the Master alone was a native of Tang who translated the scriptures of the West; he is thus the patriarch of the Ci'en school of the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) tradition.
The *Heart Sūtra* is especially the sovereign of the entire Great Canon; none but one who has "poured out the entire canon" could annotate even a single word of it. Only...
The Great Master Boting has lain his heart within the treasury of the teachings for fifty years. Having completed commentaries on all the various sutras, he finally reached the Heart Sutra.

He provides one interpretation based on the principle that its essence is the rational nature, and another based on the function that it is the contemplation of phenomena; thus, essence and function are harmoniously integrated, and nature and appearance are mutually permeated.
He was truly a great meritorious minister of Ci’en Monastery. His dharma-brother, Shao Taigu, respectfully wrote this preface to the *Mahāsattva-bhāṣita-citta-sūtra*.

This sūtra spoken by the Great Sage is for the purpose of liberating all minds. Sentient beings are deluded regarding their own minds and thus receive the substance of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Sunk in the river of craving, tossed by winds and waves, they drift into the ocean of suffering and fail to attain liberation; their grief is in vain.
The Bodhisattva awakens the mind and boards the vessel of Prajñā, coming from this shore, not dwelling in the midstream, and crossing over to the other shore.
Sovereign and carefree is true, eternal bliss. Since delusion and enlightenment differ, suffering and joy are each distinct.

Regarding the defilement and purity of cause and effect, and the identity or difference between the living being and the Buddha—the Tathāgata takes pity on them and, manifesting the fruit while practicing the cause, turns the Wheel of Dharma once more for those of the nine realms.
Directly pointing to the mind of prajñā’s numinous awareness, and revealing the nature of pāramitā practice: the mind returns to wondrous enlightenment and true emptiness;
the nature reverts to nirvāṇa and quiescent extinction. There is neither ordinary person nor sage; what Buddha and what sentient being? All dharmas are empty in their marks.
The explanation of the Heart Sūtra is concluded. While the meaning is indeed as stated above, the text itself has not yet been fully addressed.

However, since the *prajñā* of words must be realized through contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*) before one can realize the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and achieve the supreme emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the present school’s method of interpreting the sūtra employs the gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*) throughout.

Even those aspects that are difficult to clarify—such as the correct measures of the holy teachings, the schools of Nature (*svabhāva*) and Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the vehicles of the Small and Great (*Hīnayāna* and *Mahāyāna*)—are each gathered [and analyzed] accordingly.

Excerpts: Every sentence clarifies and purifies. Whether concerning the patriarchal edicts or the Buddha’s teachings, the meanings of the treatises or the mantras, every dharma is followed and relied upon; every chapter provides scriptural authority.

Only then does one bring phenomena back to principle, merging them so they interpenetrate and reveal their common nature. Since the nature of words is empty, this commentary on the Buddha’s sutras with the mind as the sub-commentary is appropriately termed the "Commentary on the Heart Sutra through the Contemplation of Phenomena.
Thus it is called: *The Commentary on the Heart Sutra through the Contemplation of Phenomena*.

△ Now, in order to explain this sutra, there is a tenfold analysis: First, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; Second, its classification within the Piṭakas and Vehicles.

1. Determining the three periods of the assembly; 2. Distinguishing the four teachings and contemplations; 3. Identifying the appropriate capacities of the recipients; 4. Clarifying the essential nature of the expressive medium; 5.

Examining the scope and limitations of the primary intent; 6. Explaining the history of the translation and its transmission; 7. Providing a general explanation of the title of the scripture; 8. Analyzing the meaning of the text in detail.
△ First, regarding the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching, there are both general and specific aspects.

The general aspect is that the Tathāgata appears in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kāraṇa*), desiring to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*).

This present sutra directly points to sentient beings so that they may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision by means of the mind of *prajñā* and true emptiness. The specific aspect has ten points, the first of which is: [text continues].

First, for the purpose of elucidating the *asādhāraṇa-prajñā* (unshared wisdom); as the Sūtra says: "Practicing profound *prajñā*. Second, for the purpose of delivering all from suffering and distress; as the Sūtra says: "Illuminating the emptiness of the five aggregates, one delivers all from suffering.

Third, for the purpose of departing from the identity of the four natures and characteristics; as the text says: "Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is precisely form," thereby transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations.

Fourth, for the purpose of ensuring that the six characteristics do not arise; [therein] arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease are all absent, such that not even a speck of dust can be established. Fifth, for...

1. To clarify that all phenomena are like illusions (meaning that the aggregates, bases, elements, worldly dharmas, the truths, conditions, and wisdom—all supramundane dharmas—are like illusory shadows, empty and without reality).

2. To manifest the true emptiness of the dharma-nature (as the text says: "All phenomena have the characteristic of emptiness; within emptiness there is no form, etc."). 3. To investigate thoroughly the three virtues of nirvāṇa.

(1) The mind is free from obstruction, fear, and delusive dreams; karmic retributions, afflictions, and hindrances are all eliminated, and one dwells peacefully in the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*. (2) Eighth, it is for the sake of realizing the three types of awakening (*tri-bodhi*) that lead to *bodhi*: self-awakening (*svabodha*), which is distinct from ordinary beings as it is free from the [deluded] mind;

awakening others (*parabodha*), which is distinct from those of the two vehicles as it is free from form (*rūpa*); and perfect awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), which is distinct from bodhisattvas as it is free from both consciousness and its objects.

(3) Ninth, it is for the sake of demonstrating the integration of the exoteric and the esoteric: the former refers to the explicit scriptures, and the latter refers to the secret mantras; both are integrated and unimpeded. (4) Tenth, it is for the sake of perfecting the fruits and virtues of merit and wisdom: through understanding the principles of the scriptural meaning, one gives rise to wisdom.

The mantras eliminate obstacles, generate merit, and bring about the two adornments of merit and wisdom, as well as the twofold fulfillment of meditative concentration and insight—the ultimate perfection of the qualities of the fruition stage. Relying upon the sūtras, these ten causes and conditions are set forth to cause this teaching to arise.
△ Second, regarding the classification by way of the Pitakas and Vehicles: it is included within the three—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—specifically under the Sūtra Piṭaka.

Within the four Pitakas of Exoteric and Esoteric Buddhism, it is subsumed under both Sūtra and Mantra (as it is neither Vinaya nor Abhidharma). Within the Great and Small Vehicles, it is subsumed under the Mahāyāna. Within the three vehicles, it is subsumed under the One Vehicle. It comprises the twelve divisions of the teaching:

*sūtra* (prose), *geya* (repetitive verse), *vyākaraṇa* (prophecy), *gāthā* (isolated verse), *udāna* (spontaneous utterance), *nidāna* (causal narrative), *avadāna* (parable), *itivṛttaka* (past events), *jātaka* (birth stories), *vaipulya* (extensive teachings), *adbhutadharma* (marvelous events), and *upadeśa* (treatises/discourses).
This is categorized within the division of the scriptures.
△ Regarding the determination by means of the three periods of assembly: among the three illuminations (initial, transformative, and returning), it was spoken during the transformative illumination.

Among the three turnings (initial, middle, and final) of the illumination, it was spoken during the final transformative illumination. Among the five assemblies (*Huayan*, *Āgama*, *Saṃdhinirmocana*, *Ghanavyūha*, and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*), it is the *Ghanavyūha*.

Regarding the ten modes of discourse— differentiation, arising and ceasing, returning to the source, non-obstruction, indeterminacy, exoteric and esoteric, sudden exposition, silence, universal inclusion, and inexhaustibility— the categories of non-obstruction and silence are subsumed within the two gates of the cosmic order (*yi*).

△ Regarding the classification of the four teachings: there are five categories of teaching. First, the Hīnayāna teaching; second, the Initial Mahāyāna teaching, also called the "Partial Teaching" (fenjiao);
third, the Final Teaching, also called the "Real Teaching" (shijiao); fourth, the Sudden One-Vehicle teaching; and fifth, the Perfect Teaching.
This present sutra properly belongs to the Sudden Teaching; it does not speak of the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) at all, but reveals only the nature of true emptiness (śūnyatā).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "In emptiness there is no form; because nothing is to be apprehended, the mind is without hindrance.

The initial statement, "Practicing the profound Prajñā, the five aggregates are all empty," encompasses both the beginning and the end of the two teachings. "This is the mark of the emptiness of all dharmas;
there is neither knowledge nor attainment" refers to the beginning. "By relying on Prajñā, one attains ultimate Nirvāṇa and realizes the three forms of Bodhi" refers to the end.

There are three types of contemplation of the Path. First is the contemplation of the Three Truths (*trīṇi satyāni*). The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) clarifies the True, the Conventional, and the Middle;

the *Rājan-vajra-cchedikā-sūtra* (Renwang jing) clarifies Emptiness, Form, and Mind, which are also termed the True, the Worldly, and the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha*). The *Brahmajāla-sūtra* clarifies the Real and the Ultimate Meaning, which are also termed the Middle Way of Emptiness and Existence.

In the present sutra, "form is not different from emptiness" refers to the contemplation of emptiness, which is the True Truth (*satya*). "Emptiness is not different from... [refers to the Conventional Truth].

Form (*rūpa*) is the contemplation of the provisional, which is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). That form is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the contemplation of the Middle Way, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Furthermore, "non-arising" and so forth are the contemplation of the true truth; "non-ceasing" and so forth are the contemplation of the conventional truth; and "the empty characteristic of all phenomena" is the contemplation of the Middle Truth within the ultimate emptiness.

Regarding these two types of emptiness, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: first, the wisdom of the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*); second, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Wisdom. There are three types of wisdom regarding emptiness: the wisdom of the emptiness of persons, the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena, and the wisdom of the emptiness of both. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* clarifies this as the emptiness of persons, the emptiness of phenomena, and the emptiness of both.

The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* refers to internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of emptiness. As the sutra says: "To perceive that the five aggregates (of the self) are all empty"—this is the contemplation of the three types of emptiness.

It is further stated: "There is neither ignorance nor attainment; because there is nothing to be attained. It is also stated: "The mind is without hindrance; because it is without hindrance. Regarding the wisdom-mind:

internally, through the contemplation of the emptiness of persons, there is neither attainment nor hindrance; externally, through the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena, there is nothing to be attained and therefore no hindrance.

When contemplating both the emptiness of emptiness, there is the non-contemplation of the three and the three. This is the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) perspective as explained in the *Dīpaśāstra*.
The contemplation on the lack of nature of the imputed, the contemplation on the lack of nature of the dependent, and the contemplation on the lack of nature of the perfected. As that verse says:

"The first is the lack of nature in terms of characteristics; the second is the lack of inherent nature; the latter [the third] is due to being far removed from the nature of the self and phenomena as they are grasped."

This is first called the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-vipaśyanā*), next called the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-vipaśyanā*), and finally called the contemplation of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-vipaśyanā*).

As the Sūtra says: "It can eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false. The elimination of distress is the contemplation of the imagined (*parikalpita-vipaśyanā*); the elimination of everything is the contemplation of the dependent (*paratantra-vipaśyanā*);

and "true" is the contemplation of the perfected (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, it says: "The mark of the emptiness of all phenomena"—this mark is precisely the contemplation of signlessness.
Dharmas are the contemplation of non-arising; emptiness is the contemplation of the absence of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, being neither arising nor ceasing, the mind is free from fear;

this is the contemplation of the true nature as the absence of intrinsic nature. Being neither defiled nor pure, the mind is free from hindrance; this is the contemplation of the arising nature as the absence of intrinsic nature.

Being neither increasing nor decreasing, the mind is free from inverted conceptions; this is the contemplation of the grasping nature as the absence of intrinsic nature. Other cases should be considered by analogy.
△ Fifth, regarding the appropriate capacity of those to be converted: the categories of sentient beings' capacities do not exceed the three groups (*tri-niyata*) and the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*).

Among the three groups—namely, the fixed-in-rightness (*samyaktva-niyata*), the fixed-in-evil (*mithyātva-niyata*), and the unfixed (*aniyata*)—this [teaching] is primarily for the unfixed, in order to refute the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) of emptiness and existence held by ordinary people and non-Buddhists.

It turns those of the two vehicles away from them and directs them toward the Mahāyāna (addressing Śāriputra). It causes provisional bodhisattvas not to be confused by emptiness (emptiness being identical to form, etc.).

It causes those of the three vehicles to enter the Middle Way of the One Vehicle (form is not different from emptiness, as well as non-arising and non-ceasing, etc.). Furthermore, it serves to establish those who are correctly settled in their resolve.

It causes the increase of sublime conduct and acts as a remote causal condition for those of false certainty. Among the five vehicles (humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas), it applies only to the bodhisattva;
for the bodhisattva practices profound *prajñā*. Among the five natures (śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, tathāgata, ...), [it applies only to the tathāgata-nature].
[The category of] the indeterminate (aniyata-gotra) is precisely that which is reached by the Tathāgata-lineage and the indeterminate nature. The text states:
"Bodhisattvas attain ultimate nirvāṇa, and all Buddhas realize *samyak-saṃbodhi*; furthermore, they act as distant causes and conditions for other natures.
Thus, it is known that whether one has heard [the Dharma] or not, whether sentient or insentient, any being endowed with the nature of *prajñā* is a recipient of the teaching.

△ Sixth, regarding the essential nature of that which expresses [the meaning]: 1. The Gate of Following Characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvartin*): The text states, "The Prajñāpāramitā mantra is spoken. Here, sound, name, phrase, and meaning are all taken as its essence.

2. The Gate of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*): The Sūtra says, "The mind is without hindrance. This implies that the preceding subject and object of expression are both transformations of one's own consciousness.
3. The Gate of Returning to Nature (*dharmatā-pratyāgama*): As stated below, "This is the mark of the emptiness of all phenomena; it is far removed from..."

When inverted dreams and delusions are overturned, then the mind-consciousness is also empty, for it is nothing other than the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding the four gates of unimpeded understanding, as it is said:
"Emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness; there is neither increase nor decrease," and so forth. Thus, one knows that Prajñā is a great divine mantra.
Consequently, the preceding states of mind, objects, phenomena, and principles are all a single, unimpeded dependent origination. Furthermore, in practicing profound Prajñā...

If one speaks of the Prajñā mantra, it refers to its characters. The essence of the first gate is to clearly perceive the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*) and to depart from inverted perceptions;
this is contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā*). The essence of the second and third gates is to deliver all beings from suffering; it is true and not false; this is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Because the latter one is the essence of the gate, this single sutra encompasses all four [aspects] completely.
△ Seventh, regarding the scope and limitations of the fundamental tenets (*śāstrārtha*): generally, there are six. First, the Hīnayāna school, which differs into twenty sections.

1. The Dharma-character school (Faxiangzong), such as the masters of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Weishi lun), including Dharmapāla and others; 2. The School that Destroys Characteristics (Poxiangzong), such as the masters of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhidu lun), including Bhāviveka and others;

3. The Mind-store school (Zangxinzong), such as the masters of the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Qixin lun), including Aśvaghoṣa and others; 4. The True-nature school (Zhenxingzong), such as the masters of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-śāstra* (Lengqie lun), including Nāgārjuna and others;
5. The Dharma-realm school (Fajiezong), such as the masters of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śāstra* (Huayan lun), including Vasubandhu and others. Now, this...

Regarding this sūtra, it is subsumed within three or five categories. Because the Prajñāpāramitā section and the nature of emptiness both apply here, the Master Jñānaprabha unified them into a single school.
To clarify the essential tenets specifically concerning this sūtra, there are further general and specific aspects. Generally, the three types of *prajñā* constitute its essential tenets;
that is, taking the textual teachings as the basis to give rise to the wisdom of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*) is the tenet. As for the realization...
Taking the true reality (*tathatā*) of ultimate emptiness as the goal, five pairs of categories are separately established: 1. **Teaching and Meaning**:

To revere the verbal teachings and explanations as the primary principle, while not grasping at the conceptual meanings of phenomena such as existence or non-existence, is the goal. 2. **Phenomena and Principle**:

To take the emptying of the phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of mundane and supramundane dharmas as the primary principle, and to reveal the rational nature of the ultimate emptiness of the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*), is the goal. 3. **Object**... [text continues]

1. Wisdom (*jñāna*): Taking as its thesis the principle-sphere of the non-characteristic nature of the emptiness of all phenomena; taking as its goal the contemplative wisdom that arises through the insight of *prajñā* to perceive the absence of views.
2. Cultivation and Realization (*bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā*): Taking as its thesis the practice of profound *prajñā* through the state of no-mind and no-wisdom;

taking as its goal the entry into the fruition-virtue of *nirvāṇa*, which is characterized by neither attainment nor grasping. 3. Essential Nature and Function (*svabhāva-kāritra*): Perfectly complete.

Bodhi takes the fundamental essence of non-attainment as its primary principle (*mūla*), and takes the great function of responding to conditions to deliver all beings from suffering as its ultimate goal (*prayojana*).
These five [stages] arise such that the subsequent and the preceding depend upon one another.
△ Eighth, regarding the transmission and circulation of the translations: there are seven translations of this sutra in total.
First, translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin, titled *Mahāprajñāpāramitāmahāvidyāmantra-sūtra*.
Second, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang, titled *Prajñāpāramitāhṛdaya-sūtra*. Third, [translated by] the Tripitaka Master from India of the Tang...
1. Translated by Amoghavajra of Great Vast Wisdom; titled in the Sanskrit manuscript as the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. 2.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmachandra from India during the Song dynasty (Fayue); titled the *Samantabhadra-jñāna-kośa-prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. 3.
Translated by the Kapiśa śramaṇa Prajña together with Liyan and others; [titled] the *Prajñā*... [text fragment].
The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Cixian of the Song dynasty; titled in the Sanskrit original as the *Bhagavatī-prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
Translated by the Indian Tripitaka Master Śīladharma of the Song dynasty; titled the *Buddhabhāṣita-ārya-buddhamātṛ-prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
The version currently transmitted in the world is the second of these seven translations. Up to...
Regarding the commentaries and sub-commentaries of past and present: there is the *Brief Commentary* by the Tang-era Tripitaka Master Xianshou;

the annotated explanation by the monks Zongle and Ruyi of Mingtian Monastery; and the textual analysis by Song Lian, Scholar-in-Ordinary of the Hanlin Academy. Other details are not recorded here at length.
△ Nine: General Explanation of the Scripture Title. (2) First, the title: *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.

This scripture takes a single dharma as its title. *Prajñā* is the essence; *pāramitā* is the function. It does not depart from the single general characteristic of the "Heart" (*hṛdaya*). Based on...
Brief Commentary. Furthermore, the title may be understood through both dharma and metaphor. The great collection of six hundred fascicles is likened to the body;
the fourteen-line minor version is likened to the mind. In Sanskrit, *prajñā* means "wisdom" (*hui*). "Wisdom" (*zhi*) carries the sense of decisive judgment;

it refers to the wondrous realization of the true source, which is exclusively determinate, for it illuminates alone with clarity. Thus, it is "prajña. "Wisdom" (*hui*) carries the sense of discernment and illumination.
To fully comprehend all phenomena, one must exercise discernment, for it is through cultivation that delusions are severed. Briefly stated, there are three aspects:

first, the *dharmatā* of true reality, which is the empty nature of phenomena that is the object of contemplation; second, contemplative illumination, which is the sublime wisdom of original enlightenment that serves as the subject of contemplation.
These are three characters. The first two characters signify the verbal teaching. In Sanskrit, this is *pāra*; here it is translated as "the other shore" (*parā*).

This refers to Great Nirvāṇa, which is translated as "Great Extinction and Deliverance" (*mahā-parinirvāṇa*). "Great" (*mahā*) is the Dharma-body; "extinction" (*nirodha*) is liberation; and "deliverance" (*nirvāṇa*) is wisdom (*prajñā*).
